title: Efron on survival, prediction, and the skewed law of expectation
summary: A study of chapter nine of Efron's 'Thinking Like a Statistician'. Survival analysis is really time-to-first-event analysis with right censoring, and the hazard-rate reformulation neutralises censoring by asking a question that only needs the data actually in hand. The chapter ends on pure prediction algorithms and the cost of deleting the mechanism from the model.
evidence: 2.5% of men die in their 91st year, but 16% of 90-year-olds die before 91: the denominator error
hazard rate at 90 is roughly 80x the hazard rate at 30 (0.16 vs 0.002 for men)
a 90-year-old carries about 438 micromorts per day, versus 1.5 for a healthy young adult
censoring was 31% in the treatment arm versus 14% in the control arm, so the better arm produced more missing data
random train/test split gave 2% test error; splitting by enrolment time gave 24% on the same data and algorithm
prostate study: 6,033 genes measured across 102 men
Pareto tail exponent a = 3 gives D = 1, the exact form of the skewed law: expected remaining wait equals the wait so far
median survival 182 days in arm A versus 324 days in arm B
notes: Efron's own text names the finance transfer: time to default, time to early repayment, time to contract termination share this structure. That sentence is the seed of the strongest bridge in the corpus.
